We're also the authors behind pgvectorscale. From our blog post:

This isn’t the first vector index we’ve built and open-sourced for PostgreSQL. In 2024, Tiger Data released pgvectorscale, which used a graph-based indexing algorithm inspired by Microsoft’s DiskANN research. We deliberately chose a disk-optimized design so that indexes could scale beyond available RAM. Our initial benchmarks were promising, but as adoption grew and we tested against a wider variety of datasets, particularly low-dimensional ones, we encountered a troubling problem: portions of the graph could become unreachable, causing recall to degrade. We searched the literature for a principled solution but couldn’t find one, and the heuristics we tried worked on some datasets but not others.

That’s a frustrating failure mode for a search index. When queries are slow, you can measure the problem and tune accordingly. But when recall degrades, you might not even notice until users start questioning the quality of their search results. And telling them to experiment with yet another set of tuning parameters isn’t the experience we want to provide.

Meanwhile, partitioned-list approaches reminiscent of IVFFlat were getting a second life, as advances in compression and optimization addressed many of their old limitations. More importantly, they offered stronger guarantees than we could achieve by patching a graph-based index. We came to believe they were a better foundation, and decided to start over.

With the introduction of pg_vectorsearch, we are shifting the majority of our vector-search development efforts to this new architecture. The existing pgvectorscale extension, which is stable and handling production workloads currently, will enter maintenance mode.

The article misses the point.

> The worst test-takers would also overestimate their performance the most because they are simply the furthest from getting a perfect score.

No. Earlier the article correctly states that all result quadrants more or less guess their raw performance with a similar degree of precision, but fail to guess their performance relative to each other with the same level of precision. These are two entirely unrelated measures that the article attempts to correlate in an invented relationship. The actual Dunning-Kruger results also indicate the highest scoring quadrant tend to understand their performance relative to their testing peers, but they are off by much less than the lowest score quadrant.

I am not saying Dunning-Kruger is necessarily correct or valid, and it has been challenged repeatedly. Still it is necessary to know what Dunning-Kruger actually concludes before challenging it.

Secondly, regardless of agreement on the conclusions provided by Dunning-Kruger it does identify something more important than relative bias. People are generally better at guessing from a known, or at least determinable, objective measure than they are at guessing from perceptive qualities that includes themselves as a data point. This is the basis of social intelligence. Social intelligence is the ability to perceive the communications of other people and to introspect. Both introspection and perception of others are required for the definition of social intelligence. Social intelligence has a weak correlation to academic intelligence as it is primarily a perceptive skill (conscientiousness) but it also requires the proper motivation (openness). People with low general intelligence are more likely to score lower in social intelligence and people with lower perceptive skills in any regard are less motivated/capable to measure things for any reason, and that motivation discrepancy is dramatically elevated a person places themselves a data point of measure.
